title: Medication Reconciliation: The List Is a Clinical Test
bottomLine: Medication reconciliation compares what the patient actually takes with what the record says and what the new clinical plan requires. It should occur at transitions of care and whenever symptoms could be medication-related.
recognize: Duplicate therapy, discontinued drugs still being taken, OTC products, supplements and multiple pharmacy records commonly create discrepancies.
differentiate: Nonadherence may be intentional, access-related, adverse-effect driven or caused by misunderstanding; it is not one behaviour.
assessment: Ask the patient or caregiver to describe actual medication name, dose, timing, indication and recent changes, including OTC, cannabis, alcohol and supplements.
workup: Verify with pharmacy, prior discharge records or specialist notes when high-risk discrepancies remain.
management: Resolve duplicates, interactions and unclear indications and produce one current list with explicit starts, stops and dose changes.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, immunosuppressants and antiepileptics deserve priority because reconciliation errors can cause rapid serious harm.
counselling: Tell patients why a medication was stopped or changed rather than relying on the printed list alone.
followUp: Ensure primary care, pharmacy and relevant specialists receive the reconciled plan.
examTrap: Copying the electronic medication list into a discharge summary without asking what the patient actually takes.
oneLinePearl: The medication list is not true until it has been reconciled with the patient.
sourceBasis: Healthcare Excellence Canada medication reconciliation principles

title: Renal Prescribing: Dose the Drug to Kidney Function and Toxicity Risk
bottomLine: Kidney impairment changes drug clearance, metabolite accumulation and electrolyte risk. Verify the renal function measure used in the product or guideline, reassess during AKI and do not assume a chronic dose remains safe when kidney function changes quickly.
recognize: Antimicrobials, gabapentinoids, digoxin, lithium, anticoagulants and many diabetes drugs have clinically important renal considerations.
differentiate: Stable CKD dosing differs from AKI because creatinine-based estimates are unreliable during rapid change.
assessment: Review baseline and current renal function, weight, age, volume status, dialysis and interacting nephrotoxins.
workup: Use drug-specific therapeutic monitoring when available and monitor potassium, renal function or levels based on the medication.
management: Adjust dose, interval or agent and re-evaluate after AKI or dialysis changes.
medicationSafety: Avoid prescribing solely from an automated eGFR alert without checking the drug's recommended renal metric and the clinical trajectory.
counselling: Explain temporary holds during dehydrating illness when appropriate and when to restart.
followUp: Set a repeat kidney-function date after starting or increasing drugs that affect kidney function or potassium.
examTrap: Continuing the same gabapentin or DOAC dose through a major acute decline in kidney function without reassessment.
oneLinePearl: Renal dosing is dynamic when renal function is dynamic.
sourceBasis: Canadian nephrology and prescribing practice principles

title: Hepatic Prescribing: Injury, Function, and Portal Physiology Matter
bottomLine: Liver disease can alter metabolism, protein binding, bleeding risk and sensitivity to sedatives. Mild aminotransferase elevation alone does not predict drug clearance; decompensated cirrhosis and impaired synthetic function require more cautious prescribing.
recognize: Ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and impaired synthetic function signal decompensated disease.
differentiate: Transaminitis is liver injury; it is not automatically liver failure.
assessment: Review cirrhosis stage, albumin/INR context, renal function, encephalopathy, alcohol and all hepatotoxic drugs/supplements.
workup: Use medication-specific liver monitoring and specialist guidance for decompensated disease or narrow-therapeutic-index drugs.
management: Avoid or reduce high-risk sedating, nephrotoxic or hepatically cleared drugs when decompensation makes harm more likely.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs are generally hazardous in decompensated cirrhosis; opioids and benzodiazepines can precipitate encephalopathy; acetaminophen can still be used at appropriate reduced total dosing in many stable liver-disease contexts rather than being universally banned.
counselling: Ask about supplements and alcohol because both can alter hepatotoxicity risk.
followUp: Monitor symptoms and labs based on the specific medication rather than indiscriminate frequent liver panels.
examTrap: Assuming acetaminophen is always forbidden in chronic liver disease while prescribing an NSAID to a patient with ascites.
oneLinePearl: Cirrhosis prescribing risk is physiology, not just ALT.

title: Medication in Pregnancy and Lactation: Compare Exposure With Untreated Disease
bottomLine: Medication decisions in pregnancy and breastfeeding compare the known or plausible treatment risk with the risk of untreated maternal disease. Automatically stopping effective therapy can be more dangerous than continuing a well-studied medication.
recognize: Timing of exposure, dose, placental transfer, neonatal effects and breastmilk exposure vary greatly between drugs.
differentiate: Teratogenic risk during organogenesis differs from late-pregnancy neonatal toxicity; breastfeeding exposure is not equivalent to in-utero exposure.
assessment: Confirm gestational/postpartum stage, indication, disease severity, prior relapse, all prescriptions/OTCs/supplements and infant prematurity or illness when breastfeeding.
workup: Use current Canadian product monographs, obstetric/teratology resources and specialist guidance rather than obsolete pregnancy-letter categories.
management: Continue, switch, taper or stop based on evidence, disease risk and patient preference; choose the lowest effective regimen without undertreating serious disease.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, valproate, isotretinoin, methotrexate and some other agents carry major pregnancy risk; many common antibiotics, antidepressants and asthma drugs can be used when clinically indicated.
redFlags: Severe maternal disease after medication cessation
Breastfeeding preterm infant with high-risk maternal drug
counselling: Discuss absolute risks and uncertainty rather than saying a drug is simply 'safe' or 'unsafe'.
followUp: Document shared decision-making and monitor maternal disease as well as fetal or infant outcomes.
examTrap: Abruptly stopping a necessary antiseizure or psychiatric medication solely because a pregnancy test is positive.
oneLinePearl: Medication safety includes the risk of not treating the parent.
sourceBasis: SOGC and Canadian perinatal pharmacology principles

title: Geriatric Pharmacology: Start With Goals, Reserve, and Adverse-Effect Syndromes
bottomLine: Older adults vary enormously in renal function, frailty, cognition and treatment goals. Prescribe from physiology and function rather than age alone, and suspect medication effects when falls, delirium, constipation, retention or orthostasis appear.
recognize: Reduced renal clearance, altered body composition and pharmacodynamic sensitivity increase adverse effects from sedatives, anticholinergics and BP-lowering drugs.
differentiate: A potentially inappropriate medication list is a screening tool, not an automatic stop list.
assessment: Review frailty, renal/hepatic function, cognition, falls, swallowing, adherence, caregiver role and treatment priorities.
workup: Use medication-specific monitoring and deprescribing trials when adverse effects are plausible.
management: Start lower when evidence supports increased sensitivity, titrate to meaningful benefit and simplify regimens.
medicationSafety: Avoid therapeutic cascades in which a drug adverse effect is treated with another drug before the culprit is recognized.
counselling: Include the patient in decisions about reducing preventive medication burden when goals or life expectancy change.
followUp: Review high-risk drugs after every major illness or hospitalization.
examTrap: Stopping an effective medication solely because it appears on an older-adult caution list without assessing indication, benefit and alternatives.
oneLinePearl: In geriatrics, medication appropriateness is individualized benefit minus individualized harm.

title: Drug Interactions: Inhibitors Raise Exposure, Inducers Lower It
bottomLine: Clinically important pharmacokinetic interactions often occur when one drug inhibits or induces the metabolism or transport of another. The consequence depends on whether the affected drug needs high exposure for efficacy or low exposure to avoid toxicity.
recognize: Strong inhibitors can rapidly increase concentrations of susceptible drugs; enzyme induction develops and resolves more slowly.
differentiate: Pharmacodynamic interactions add effects without changing concentration, such as multiple sedatives or QT-prolonging drugs.
assessment: Review all prescriptions, OTCs, herbal products, grapefruit or other relevant foods and recent starts/stops.
workup: Use a reliable interaction database or product monograph for high-risk combinations rather than memory alone.
management: Avoid, substitute, dose-adjust or monitor based on interaction severity and therapeutic index.
medicationSafety: Warfarin, DOACs, calcineurin inhibitors, antiseizure drugs and some antiarrhythmics are especially sensitive to clinically important interactions.
counselling: Tell patients to check before starting supplements or OTCs when they take high-risk interacting drugs.
followUp: Reassess after both starting and stopping an interacting drug because exposure can change in either direction.
examTrap: Stopping a strong enzyme inducer without considering that concentrations of the other drug may then rise and become toxic.
oneLinePearl: Interactions change when the interacting drug starts—and again when it stops.

title: QT Prolongation: Drug Stack Plus Electrolytes Plus Susceptibility
bottomLine: Torsades risk reflects QTc duration plus drug burden, potassium and magnesium, bradycardia, structural heart disease and congenital susceptibility. Avoid stacking QT-prolonging drugs when safer alternatives exist and correct reversible risks.
recognize: Macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antiemetics, antipsychotics, methadone and antiarrhythmics are common contributors.
differentiate: A prolonged QT is a risk marker; torsades is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia syndrome.
assessment: Review syncope/family sudden death, all QT drugs, electrolytes, bradycardia and baseline ECG when risk warrants.
workup: Obtain ECG and potassium/magnesium when starting or combining high-risk therapy in susceptible patients.
management: Stop or substitute offending drugs, correct electrolytes and treat torsades urgently with magnesium and rate/electrical strategies according to acute protocol.
medicationSafety: Automated QTc can be inaccurate in irregular rhythms or wide QRS and may require clinician correction/interpretation.
counselling: Warn high-risk patients to check interactions before new antibiotics or antiemetics.
followUp: Repeat ECG after meaningful risk modification when clinically indicated.
examTrap: Prescribing a QT-prolonging antibiotic plus antiemetic to a patient with hypokalemia and a markedly prolonged baseline QT without reassessment.
oneLinePearl: Torsades is often a stack of small risks.
sourceBasis: Canadian cardiovascular and pharmacology practice principles

title: Opioid Analgesia: Indication, Functional Goal, Risk, and Exit Plan
bottomLine: Opioids can be appropriate for selected acute, cancer, palliative and carefully selected chronic pain, but every prescription needs an indication, expected benefit, risk assessment, co-sedative review and a plan for duration or reassessment.
recognize: Respiratory disease, sleep apnea, older age, renal/hepatic dysfunction, benzodiazepines/alcohol and prior overdose increase harm risk.
differentiate: Physical dependence is expected with prolonged exposure and is not the same as opioid use disorder.
assessment: Define pain diagnosis and functional goals, prior therapies, substance use, mental health, medications, renal/hepatic function and pregnancy.
workup: Prescription monitoring and urine testing are used selectively according to jurisdiction and risk; they do not replace therapeutic alliance or clinical assessment.
management: Use nonopioid and nonpharmacologic options when effective, lowest effective opioid exposure for necessary duration, and naloxone or OAT when overdose/OUD risk requires it.
medicationSafety: Avoid opioid-benzodiazepine combinations when possible; methadone and fentanyl have unique potency and kinetic risks; renal impairment changes opioid metabolite safety.
counselling: Discuss driving, constipation, safe storage and the difference between tolerance/dependence and addiction.
followUp: Reassess pain, function and harm; taper gradually when long-term therapy no longer has net benefit unless immediate safety requires a different plan.
examTrap: Abruptly stopping long-term opioids in a stable patient solely because the dose is considered high, without a safety or taper plan.
oneLinePearl: Opioid prescribing needs a beginning, a reason and an exit strategy.
sourceBasis: Canadian opioid-prescribing and pain practice resources

title: Insulin Safety: Match Insulin Action to Food, Glucose, and Illness
bottomLine: Insulin is a high-alert medication. Know which dose is basal, prandial and correctional, verify concentration and device, and adjust for intake, activity, illness and renal function without omitting essential basal insulin in type 1 diabetes.
recognize: Hypoglycemia is the most immediate common harm; medication reconciliation errors can confuse similarly named products and concentrated formulations.
differentiate: Sliding-scale-only reactive treatment is not equivalent to a physiologic basal-prandial regimen for patients who need basal insulin.
assessment: Review actual product/device, dose/timing, meals, glucose/CGM, hypoglycemia, renal function and sick-day plan.
workup: Use glucose patterns rather than a single value to adjust chronic dosing; check ketones during illness or significant hyperglycemia in type 1 diabetes.
management: Teach injection technique, rotation, storage and hypoglycemia treatment and ensure glucagon access when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Double-check units and concentration; never write ambiguous abbreviations for units; pump failure in type 1 diabetes requires rapid backup insulin planning.
counselling: Teach that basal insulin and meal insulin have different jobs.
followUp: Review data soon after significant regimen changes.
examTrap: Holding all insulin in a fasting patient with type 1 diabetes rather than adjusting the regimen while preserving basal insulin.
oneLinePearl: Basal insulin covers biology; prandial insulin covers food.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada insulin and type 1 diabetes guidance

title: Anticoagulants: Indication, Kidney Function, Interactions, Bleeding, Procedures
bottomLine: Safe anticoagulation requires the correct indication, dose for renal and patient factors, interaction review, bleeding assessment and a documented procedure plan. Do not reduce DOAC dose simply because bleeding risk feels high unless the drug-specific criteria are met.
recognize: AF stroke prevention, VTE treatment and mechanical valve anticoagulation are different indications with different drug options.
differentiate: DOACs are generally not used for mechanical heart valves; warfarin remains required in several specific conditions.
assessment: Review indication, last dose, renal/hepatic function, age/weight criteria when relevant, antiplatelets/NSAIDs, adherence and bleeding.
workup: Routine INR monitoring does not measure DOAC effect; use drug-specific laboratory strategies only when clinically needed.
management: Follow current Thrombosis Canada guidance for dosing, interruption, reversal and restarting after bleeding or procedures.
medicationSafety: Underdosing can cause stroke/VTE while overdosing causes bleeding; do not use off-label 'safer' reduced doses without criteria.
counselling: Teach missed-dose instructions, bleeding signs and why NSAIDs or OTC products matter.
followUp: Reassess renal function, adherence and bleeding periodically.
examTrap: Reducing apixaban dose solely because the patient is 78 and you are worried about falls, without meeting dose-reduction criteria.
oneLinePearl: Anticoagulant safety requires the right dose—not simply a lower dose.

title: Systemic Corticosteroids: Powerful, Useful, and Not Benign
bottomLine: Systemic corticosteroids rapidly suppress inflammation but increase glucose, BP, infection, mood, bone and adrenal risks. Use the lowest effective exposure for the indicated disease and recognize that prolonged therapy may suppress the HPA axis.
recognize: Hyperglycemia, insomnia/mood change, fluid retention, infection and dyspepsia can occur quickly; osteoporosis, cataract and adrenal suppression increase with cumulative exposure.
differentiate: Withdrawal symptoms and adrenal insufficiency can mimic relapse after abrupt cessation of prolonged therapy.
assessment: Review indication, dose/duration, diabetes, infection, bone risk, mood/psychosis, vaccines and concurrent immunosuppression.
workup: Monitor glucose/BP and longer-term bone/eye risk according to exposure; assess adrenal suppression when clinically relevant.
management: Use steroid-sparing treatment when appropriate and taper based on duration, disease control and adrenal risk rather than a universal schedule.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy when adrenal suppression is possible; live-vaccine timing can be affected by immunosuppressive dosing.
counselling: Teach sick-day or stress-dose instructions when adrenal suppression is established or strongly suspected.
followUp: Review whether each repeat burst can be prevented with better disease control.
examTrap: Prescribing repeated steroid bursts for asthma or arthritis without recognizing cumulative toxicity and inadequate controller therapy.
oneLinePearl: Every steroid burst has a benefit—and a cumulative cost.
sourceBasis: Canadian endocrine and specialty prescribing principles

title: Immunosuppression: Screen Infection, Vaccinate Early, Monitor the Drug
bottomLine: Biologics, targeted immune therapies and conventional immunosuppressants have therapy-specific infection, malignancy, laboratory and vaccine risks. Before treatment, establish baseline infection/vaccine status and create a monitoring plan rather than using one generic 'immunosuppressed' checklist.
recognize: TB, hepatitis B and opportunistic-infection risks vary substantially by mechanism.
differentiate: Live-vaccine restrictions and vaccine-response impairment differ by drug and timing.
assessment: Review infection history, TB/HBV risk, vaccines, pregnancy, cancer history, liver/renal function and concurrent immune therapies.
workup: Use drug-specific CBC, liver/renal, TB, HBV and other baseline/ongoing tests based on current specialty guidance.
management: Update vaccines before therapy when feasible, counsel on serious infection signs and coordinate temporary holds during selected severe infections or procedures according to the specific drug.
medicationSafety: Do not stop chronic immunosuppression automatically for every mild infection or vaccine; inappropriate interruption can cause disease flare or organ rejection.
counselling: Tell patients which vaccines and infections require contacting the specialty team.
followUp: Track monitoring dates and avoid therapy continuation when required safety labs are missing.
examTrap: Giving a live vaccine without checking whether the patient's biologic creates a contraindicating level of immunosuppression.

title: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring: Time the Level to the Pharmacology
bottomLine: A drug level is interpretable only when you know dose, formulation, sampling time, steady state, renal or hepatic change and the clinical question. Random levels can mislead more than they help.
recognize: Lithium, digoxin, selected antiseizure drugs, aminoglycosides and vancomycin are common monitoring contexts, but contemporary strategies differ by drug.
differentiate: A therapeutic population range does not guarantee efficacy or exclude toxicity in an individual patient.
assessment: Document last dose and sample time, adherence, interacting drugs, renal function, toxicity symptoms and reason for testing.
workup: Use trough, timed post-dose or model-based monitoring according to the medication and current protocol.
management: Adjust treatment using the level plus symptoms, organ function and indication rather than treating the laboratory number alone.
medicationSafety: Acute kidney injury can make a previously stable drug level dangerous; interacting drugs can alter levels abruptly.
counselling: Teach patients when to hold or seek advice during dehydration for high-risk drugs such as lithium.
followUp: Repeat levels after dose, interaction or organ-function changes at an interpretable time.
examTrap: Increasing a medication because a 'low level' was drawn two hours before the intended trough and the patient is clinically controlled.
oneLinePearl: A drug level without a dose time is half a test.

title: Controlled Substances: Therapeutic Care With Regulatory and Diversion Safeguards
bottomLine: Prescribing controlled substances requires the same patient-centred diagnostic rigor as other medicines plus jurisdiction-specific regulatory, documentation and diversion safeguards. A controlled-drug label does not justify stigma or abandonment.
recognize: Opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines and some other controlled drugs have misuse, dependence or diversion risks but can also be appropriate treatment.
differentiate: Physiologic dependence and tolerance are not the same as substance use disorder; aberrant behaviour may reflect undertreated disease, access barriers or diversion and needs assessment.
assessment: Confirm indication, alternatives, substance history, overdose risk, mental health, pharmacy/prescriber overlap and patient treatment goals.
workup: Use prescription-monitoring programs, urine testing or treatment agreements when clinically justified and permitted, not as punitive surveillance.
management: Prescribe the minimum appropriate quantity and monitoring intensity for risk, coordinate one clear prescriber/pharmacy plan when useful and treat identified SUD rather than abruptly terminating care.
medicationSafety: Controlled-substance rules, NP authority, e-prescribing and monitoring obligations vary by province, territory and drug and must be checked locally.
counselling: Discuss storage, driving, sharing prohibition and disposal without shaming the patient.
followUp: Document benefit, function, adverse effects and risk mitigation at meaningful intervals.
examTrap: Dismissing a patient from care immediately after an unexpected urine result without confirming the result or assessing for substance use disorder.
oneLinePearl: Risk management should make controlled prescribing safer, not punitive.
sourceBasis: provincial and territorial nursing regulator requirements
